about: Warning signs of government imposter scams about Social Security, Medicare, SNAP, Medicaid and housing help, in the words of the agencies and the FTC. Used by the on-device check; a message is never called genuine.

rows.ask: It told me to pay with gift cards, a prepaid card, cryptocurrency, a wire transfer, gold or cash
rows.plain: Scammers tell you to pay in a specific way. Social Security says: do not pay with gift cards, precious metals, prepaid debit cards, cryptocurrency, wire transfers or cash.

other.plain: No government agency will demand that you pay with gift cards, a wire transfer, cryptocurrency or a payment app. Only a scammer insists on that.

rows.ask: It threatened me or said I must act right away
rows.plain: Scammers pressure you to act immediately. Social Security will never threaten, scare or pressure you to take an immediate action.

other.plain: Real government staff won't call to threaten to arrest you, freeze your accounts or take your property, even if you owe money.

rows.ask: It said there is a problem with my number, card, account or benefits, or that I won something
rows.plain: Scammers claim there is a problem or a prize.

other.plain: Scammers pretend to be from an agency you know, often saying there is a problem or a prize. The FTC notes that it, for one, never runs sweepstakes or lotteries.

rows.ask: It asked for my Social Security number, Medicare number, bank details, card number or a password
rows.plain: Social Security will never ask for sensitive or personal information through social media, email or text message.

other.plain: Government agencies will never call, email, text, or message you on social media to ask for money or personal information.

rows.ask: It told me to move my money somewhere to keep it safe
rows.plain: Social Security and its Inspector General will never ask you to transfer money to protect it.

other.plain: No one from the government will tell you to move your money to keep it safe. Only a scammer will.

rows.ask: Someone wants to meet me or send a courier to collect cash, cards or gold
rows.plain: They will never meet you in person to exchange cash, gift cards, cryptocurrency or gold bars.

other.plain: Someone who works for the government won't tell you to get cash or gold and give it to someone.

rows.ask: It told me to keep this secret
rows.plain: They will never require you to keep information secret or confidential.

other.plain: Scammers often tell you to keep the conversation secret from your friends and family.

rows.ask: It sent a photo of a badge or an ID card
rows.plain: Federal law enforcement will never send photographs of credentials or badges to demand any kind of payment.

other.plain: Federal law enforcement will never send photographs of credentials or badges to demand any kind of payment.

rows.ask: It has a link or an attachment I was told to open
rows.plain: Social Security's advice for a suspicious message: do not click links or open attachments.

other.plain: Don't click on links in unexpected emails or text messages.

rows.plain: Pause. Hang up or ignore the message. Do not click links or open attachments, do not pay, and do not share personal information with an unexpected contact about a problem you do not recognize.
Report a Social Security-related scam to the Inspector General.
To check whether a letter or call is real, contact Social Security yourself, using the phone number or website you look up yourself and not one given in the message.

rows.ask: Someone said they were from Medicare and tried to sell me something, or wanted to come to my home
rows.plain: Medicare will not call you to sell you anything, and will not visit your home.

rows.ask: A caller I did not call first asked for my Medicare number or other personal details
rows.plain: Medicare will not call you or ask for personal information, except in limited cases, such as returning a call you made or after you reported fraud.

rows.ask: It offered free equipment, tests, care or a gift if I share my Medicare number
rows.plain: Medicare's advice: don't accept money or gifts in exchange for free medical care, and share your Medicare number only with your doctor or people who should have it.

rows.ask: It wanted me to join or switch a Medicare plan on a call I did not ask for
rows.plain: Medicare's advice: don't join a Medicare health or drug plan over the phone unless you called and asked for help.

rows.ask: It asked for my EBT card number or PIN
rows.plain: State agencies and EBT processors will never call or text to ask for your PIN or card number.

rows.ask: It says my EBT card is locked or my benefits are stopped, and gives a number or link to fix it
rows.plain: USDA has warned of fake text messages saying a SNAP EBT card has been locked, with a phone number to call for help.

rows.ask: It asked me to pay, or for card or bank details, to keep, renew or restart Medicaid
rows.plain: Medicaid won't charge you to renew or enroll. A state Medicaid program will never threaten you, or ask for your credit card information or a payment, to keep or qualify for coverage.

rows.ask: It asks for a fee to apply, or to get on a Section 8 or housing waiting list
rows.plain: Never pay anyone to be added to an assisted housing waitlist. Housing authorities and government agencies will never ask you to pay to join a waitlist or to be admitted to a housing assistance program.

rows.ask: Someone contacted me by phone, email or social media to suggest I join a waiting list
rows.plain: Housing authorities do not charge fees, and they won't reach out to you by phone or email to suggest that you join a waiting list.

To check, call Medicare yourself at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227), or look at your claims in your Medicare.gov account. If it is about a Medicare Advantage or drug plan, call the number on your plan card.
Report Medicare fraud to 1-800-MEDICARE or to the HHS Office of Inspector General. For a Medicare Advantage or drug plan, you can also call the I-MEDIC line, 1-877-772-3379.
If you are not sure a message about SNAP is real, contact your local SNAP office yourself. In Florida that is DCF at (850) 300-4323. For other states, find your state's contact in USDA's directory.
If you think you were caught by a SNAP scam or your benefits were stolen, tell your local SNAP office right away and change your PIN. Report scam texts to the Federal Trade Commission.

To check a message about Medicaid, contact your state Medicaid agency yourself, using the number on your Medicaid card or the state's own website. In Florida, eligibility is handled by DCF: (850) 300-4323.
Report a Medicaid scam to the Federal Trade Commission and to your state.
To get on a real waiting list, contact your local housing authority yourself and ask how to apply. It is free.
Report a housing voucher scam to the HUD Office of Inspector General hotline, 1-800-347-3735, and to the Federal Trade Commission.
Contact the agency yourself, using a phone number or website you look up yourself, not one given in the message.
Report imposter scams to the Federal Trade Commission.
